extracted.intended_audience: readers of 18th-century scientific correspondence / natural philosophers and educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Letter-essay style natural philosophy on atmospheric phenomena (whirlwinds, spouts, evaporation) explaining causes by observation, experiment, analogy, and hypothesis. Practical and theoretical remarks intended for other learned correspondents and general educated readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hypothesis from established fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label speculative explanations as hypotheses and avoid asserting them as certain when data are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin repeatedly frames proposed mechanisms as 'I suppose', 'I offer only as an hypothesis', and admits lack of sufficient facts; instructs modesty and submission to candid examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base explanations on observations and eyewitness accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor theoretical accounts in reported observations and descriptions from witnesses or prior authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Dr. Stuart's and Dr. Mather's accounts of spouts/whirlwinds and uses those reports to test and illustrate the proposed mechanism (e.g., tube appearance, 'bush' at foot of column).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with simple repeatable experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, perform and describe small experiments that others can repeat to test claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit thermometer experiment (wetting with spirit and blowing) showing temperature drop; gives apparatus details and measured degree changes as an example of replicable method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanistic, physically plausible reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain phenomena by invoking physical mechanisms (pressure, rarefaction, centrifugal force, evaporation) and tracing causal chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains whirlwinds by heated air rising, surrounding heavier air flowing in, formation of a central rarefied column and spiral ascent, centrifugal effects ejecting debris, and condensation producing visible tube.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ familiar analogies and thought-experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use everyday analogies (water in a tub, chimney draft, canal gate) to render abstract mechanisms intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares whirl formation to whirl in a water tub, spiral descent of water through a hole, chimney draft to explain successive motion; uses canal/gate analogy for propagation of storm onset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify where reasonable and report approximate measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Give quantitative estimates or proportions when possible to make arguments testable or concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers rough measures (e.g., water may rise near 32 feet in vacuum, storm beginning later by ~an hour per 100 miles) and diameters of columns as reported by observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe and refer to figures to clarify spatial relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include schematic figures or refer to numbered figures to explain geometry and sections of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers to Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 to explain plan/groundplot, central vacuum, and elevation of water-spout; uses labelled points (P, W, a a a a, b b b b) to ground the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address and attempt to answer reasonable objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate plausible counter-arguments or puzzling observations and attempt to resolve them within the proposed framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers the objection about why rains are not salty when water is carried up, discusses salt behavior versus water in evaporation and adhesion to air, and notes limits of his answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare alternative hypotheses and acknowledge limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast your account with other hypotheses, note where you are unconvinced, and indicate topics needing more facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly contrasts his ascending-whirl explanation with another author's descending-spout hypothesis, admits not yet satisfied, and promises further consideration; repeatedly notes insufficient facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect theory to practical implications or experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate theoretical discussion into pragmatic advice or experimental suggestions when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests practical experiments (thermometer wetting, bathing in seawater to relieve thirst), and discusses maritime dangers of spouts and possible effects on ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, modest rhetorical tone and invite critical review
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with civility, modesty, and an invitation to scrutiny; avoid overclaiming and encourage peers to examine the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closes with 'I submit to your candid examination' and 'I will consider it farther', modeling the rhetorical stance for scientific correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite prior authorities and compile multiple reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Support an account by gathering and citing previous writings and multiple observers rather than relying on a single report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References transactions, voyages (Dampier), and letters from various colonies; aggregates colonial reports of storm timings to infer propagation pattern.
